extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and articulating obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, including when to combine prior art, when substitutions are predictable, how to treat analogous art and teaching away, and how to weigh secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require articulated reasoning for obviousness rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; instead, there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should provide a reasoned explanation for every obviousness rejection (citing KSR and In re Kahn). Do not rely on conclusory labels — explicate the factual findings and the rationale tying them to the legal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: When combining prior art elements, show predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper rejection based on the rationale that the claimed invention is a combination of prior art elements also includes a finding that results flowing from the combination would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If results would not have been predictable, Office personnel should not enter an obviousness rejection using the combination-of-elements rationale and should withdraw such a rejection if it has been made (see Crocs example where combination yielded more than predictable results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution rationale (requirements for substitution rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on simple substitution of one known element for another, Office personnel must articulate specific findings resolving the Graham factual inquiries and the following four points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four findings to articulate are: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a device which differed from the claimed device by substitution of components; (2) a finding that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have substituted one known element for another and the results of the substitution would have been predictable; and (4) whatever additional Graham-based findings are necessary given the facts of the case. If any cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success / not mere 'obvious to try'
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be supported where there was a reasonable expectation of success; mere statements that it was 'obvious to try' without more are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness does not require absolute predictability of success (In re O’Farrell). Demonstrate that one skilled in the art would have known how to carry out the modification and would have had a reasonable expectation of success (examples: O’Farrell, Fout, ICON).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider capabilities of a person of ordinary skill (optimization)
rubrics_metrics.description: When claimed differences are attainable by routine optimization, the knowing ability of a person of ordinary skill to adjust parameters can support an obviousness conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If optimization of application parameters was within the level of ordinary skill, an obviousness finding is more likely (Ecolab: expert admitted one skilled in the art would know how to adjust parameters and determine optimum values). Assess whether parameter tuning would have been routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away weighs against obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art discourages, criticizes, or teaches away from the proposed modification or combination, that teaching can support nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference that warns that a proposed modification would cause failure or otherwise counsels against the change can indicate the combination would not have been made (DePuy/Puno example). Teaching away plus secondary considerations (failure by others, copying) can further support nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art: determine reasonable pertinence to problem solved
rubrics_metrics.description: References outside the applicant's field may be applied if they are reasonably pertinent to the problem the inventor was trying to solve; KSR directs a broad construction of analogous art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the problem to be solved rather than formal field labels (ICON: bed-retaining mechanisms applied to treadmills). Even if a reference is in a different field, it may be analogous if it addresses a similar problem or is reasonably pertinent to that problem (Wyers, ICON).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ignore modifications skilled artisans would make
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying a reference from a different field, an assessment must account for the modifications a person skilled in the art would make so as not to mischaracterize a teaching as teaching away or inoperable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume inoperability simply because a reference uses different component sizes or extremes; one skilled in the art would size/adapt components appropriately (ICON discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate motivation to combine (including common sense and market forces)
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness rejection based on combining references requires a clear articulation of why a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine the teachings — motivation may come from technical reasoning, common sense, or market/economic considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR and subsequent cases permit recourse to logic, judgment, and common sense where appropriate (Wyers). Market pressures, convenience, known needs, or explicit teachings can supply the 'apparent reason to combine' (Ecolab, Wyers, Muniauction). Always articulate the reason(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect elements to maintain respective properties/functions after combination
rubrics_metrics.description: A hallmark of a proper obviousness rejection based on combining known elements is a finding that one of ordinary skill would have reasonably expected the elements to maintain their respective properties or functions after combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the combined elements would simply perform as they did separately and yield predictable results, that supports obviousness (Sundance example). Explain why the properties/functions would be maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results or 'more than predictable results' favor nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If a combination yields more than predictable results or an unexpected advantage, that supports nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the combination produced results beyond what a skilled artisan would have predicted (Crocs: combination yielded improved comfort due to friction behavior; such unexpected benefits weigh against an obviousness conclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of a previously unknown problem supports nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee discovered a problem not recognized in the prior art, there may have been no reason for a skilled artisan to make the modification, supporting nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omeprazole example: adverse interaction/stability problem was not disclosed in prior art, so adding a subcoating would not have been an expected modification despite being technologically possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations require a nexus and coextensiveness to claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness (copying, praise, commercial success, skepticism) must have a nexus to the claimed invention and be coextensive with the claim scope to carry substantial weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the proffered evidence is not coextensive with the claims or lacks nexus, it will be entitled to less weight (Muniauction: evidence lacked nexus and thus did not overcome the obviousness showing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical/lead-compound considerations: structural similarity and expectation of similar properties
rubrics_metrics.description: In chemical arts, the selection of a lead compound and structural similarity can provide a reason to modify prior art compounds; an expectation of similar properties can suffice even absent explicit prior-art teaching to purify or modify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rigidly require explicit teaching to isolate a stereoisomer or modify a lead compound (Aventis). However, address whether there was a reason to modify the lead compound and whether the result would have been predictable (Eisai: absence of a reason to modify can support nonobviousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve the Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness determinations must resolve the Graham factors: scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and claims, level of ordinary skill in the art, and secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many of the specific rationales (substitution, combination, analogous art) require explicit findings on the Graham factors to support the legal conclusion (see admonition in subsection B and throughout examples).
